sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**

All eight checklist lines are yes. One problem in the copy falls outside the checklist:

1. *(No checklist line: the words.)* The facts a passenger acts on are vague. The first paragraph (x 120–775, y 150–230) says the ferry runs "every forty minutes between early morning and late evening" but gives no first or last sailing time and no departure minutes. A reader can't tell whether 06:00 or 08:00 counts as early, or whether they can still catch a boat at 21:30. That is the question that strands people. The winter note (y 362–382) says "Timetables change in winter" but not when winter starts or what changes, so the reader can't tell whether today's sailings are affected. Times and dates are what people remember and later hold the operator to, so vague wording here is a defect, not a matter of style. Fix: give the first and last sailing times, or at least the departure pattern from each landing (for example ":00 and :40 past"), and give the date range for the winter timetable. Defect. Weight: major. Fixing it would change whether a passenger can plan a crossing from this page alone.

**What's working.**
- **One idea, said plainly.** The heading "Notes for ferry passengers" (x 120–593, y 82–122) tells a stranger in one glance what this is and who it's for. The three blocks below it cover when, bikes, and a caveat, and none of them strays from that.
- **Nothing extra.** There are no rules, boxes, icons or decoration. The one font and the near-black on white suit a practical public notice, so the page holds together without any styling to make it do so.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 8 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

I've finished the walk and read the entries, and I'm writing the report now.

**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Below the first element, can you tell each level of the text (title, headings, body, captions) from the next at a glance, with no two sizes almost the same?** No.
   - **Where:** The last paragraph, "Timetables change in winter. Check the noticeboard at the landing before you travel." (x≈120–757, y≈362–382).
   - **What the viewer sees:** This line is set at about 16 px. The two paragraphs above it are about 20 px. All three are in the same typeface, weight and dark grey, with the same paragraph gap. So it doesn't read as its own level, like a caption or a notice. It reads as one more body paragraph that came out a bit smaller, and it looks like fine print. Shrinking it also makes it look like the least important line, but it is the only one that asks the passenger to do something: check the noticeboard before travelling. A skimming reader is most likely to skip the one line that could leave them stranded in winter.
   - **Why:** This is a paragraph-text block with no heading role, set a little smaller than the blocks next to it. That matches the "Sizes come from a scale" entry: a size picked on its own rather than from a deliberate scale (Bringhurst, *The Elements of Typographic Style*, 3.1.1, "Don't compose without a scale"). A difference of one size step with nothing else changed is the weak contrast Dair warns about: it looks like an accident, not a choice (Dair, *Design with Type*, ch. 8).
   - **Fix:** Make it the same size as the body, or make it a deliberate level that stands out by more than a smaller size. A short bold lead-in ("Winter timetables:") or a set-off notice would mark it as something to act on. Don't make it smaller than the information it qualifies.
   - **Kind:** Defect, because it hides the one action line, and convention (the type scale).
   - **Weight:** Major. On a page this short, this warning is a large share of what the passenger needs to take away.

**What's working.** The title is the clear place to start. At about 40 px and bold, against about 20 px regular body text, it beats the body on both size and weight, so the entry point is never in doubt. The two body paragraphs are set the same, so they read as one level of equal facts.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Nothing in this section.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 2 yes, 1 no (each level of text distinct, no two sizes almost the same).

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does the visual weight balance, with no side, crowded or empty, that makes the page look about to tip?** No. All the content sits in the upper-left: a block about 660×300 px from x≈120–780 and y≈80–385. The right 40% (x≈790–1280) and the bottom half (y≈390–800) are empty, and nothing there counters the dark bold heading or the three text blocks. The page looks like it is tipping up and to the left, and it reads as unfinished, like a page that hasn't loaded or a fragment pasted onto a canvas too big for it. It doesn't read as a deliberately open layout. The empty space is gathered into one area, which is right, but nothing gives it a job against the text, so it reads as leftover rather than as counterform. Arnheim (*Art and Visual Perception*, ch. I "Balance") says a heavy side needs a counterweight. Fix direction: if this is a web page, keep the measure-driven column (its line length is good) and anchor it, either by centering the column in the viewport or by giving the right side something that belongs there, such as the timetable, a route map, or the winter notice set as a sidebar. If this is a fixed frame like a card, slide or sign, size the frame to the content or set the text so it fills the frame. Convention (Arnheim). Weight: minor. Every line is easy to read and the order is clear, so the imbalance costs the piece finish and confidence, not comprehension.

**What's working.**
- Everything aligns exactly to one left edge at x≈120: the heading, both paragraphs and the small note. There are no near-misses, so the column reads as one clean, deliberate block.
- The spacing groups the content correctly. Lines within a paragraph sit closer (≈28 px pitch) than the paragraphs sit to each other, and the heading is close to the body it introduces. The smaller winter note is set off by size, not by an awkward gap, so it reads as an aside in the same flow.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Whether this is a wide-viewport capture of a responsive page. If the column is left-pinned at every width, the imbalance gets worse on wider screens and goes away on narrow ones. Check it at a few viewport widths in a browser.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 12 yes, 1 no (visual weight balances)

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **Comfortable reading:** The body paragraphs (about 19 px, x 120–775, y 150–335) run at roughly 60–75 characters per line with spacing of about 1.5, so each line ends and the next begins without effort. That's the range Bringhurst recommends for measure and leading.
- **Clean paragraphs:** They're set flush left with a gentle rag, marked by space only, and no line ends on a single word. The block reads as two clean, separate thoughts.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 30 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Color: applies. The piece has color, but only neutral text on a white background, so most lines pass because there is nothing to get wrong.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **A single dark gray on white.** The title, body and footnote (x≈120–790, y≈80–385) all use one near-black gray on a white field. With one ink there is nothing to clash or vibrate, and nothing competes with the words. That suits a passenger notice that people read and don't scan. Color can't mislead anyone here.
- **Strong light-to-dark contrast.** Dark text on white keeps the structure clear in grayscale. Contrast doesn't separate any levels. The 2–3 type sizes and the bold title do that job, so a reader with low vision or a color-vision deficiency loses nothing. The winter-timetable warning at y≈372 is set in the same ink as the body. It doesn't depend on a color it lacks to be noticed. Whether it needs more emphasis is a hierarchy question, not a color one.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure.
